name: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders

clinicalPearls: Trigeminal neuralgia produces brief (seconds to a minute or two) paroxysms of excruciating, superficial, stabbing pain usually in the lips, gums, cheek, or chin (V2/V3); ophthalmic-division (V1) involvement is rare. Attacks may be triggered by light tactile stimuli at facial, lip, or tongue trigger zones (washing, brushing teeth, a draft of air) and by speaking, chewing, or smiling.

An essential diagnostic feature of classic trigeminal neuralgia is the ABSENCE of demonstrable objective sensory loss on examination; demonstrable trigeminal sensory or motor deficit instead points to a structural trigeminal neuropathy or secondary cause.

Trigeminal neuralgia is relatively common (incidence ~4–8 per 100,000/year), affects mainly middle-aged and elderly persons, and roughly 60% of cases occur in women; bouts persist for weeks to months and tend to remit then recur.

When trigeminal neuralgia occurs in a young adult or is bilateral, suspect multiple sclerosis (demyelinating plaque near the trigeminal root entry zone in the pons), especially if subtle facial sensory loss is present.

Bell’s palsy is the most common form of facial paralysis (annual incidence ~25 per 100,000; lifetime risk ~1 in 60); onset is abrupt with maximal weakness by 48 h, often preceded by retroauricular pain for a day or two, and may include loss of taste and hyperacusis.

A peripheral (lower motor neuron) facial palsy weakens the whole hemiface including the forehead and eyelid closure, whereas a supranuclear (central) lesion relatively spares the forehead and orbicularis oculi because upper-face muscles receive bilateral corticobulbar innervation.

Localizing the seventh-nerve lesion: loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue points to a middle-ear-segment lesion; hyperacusis indicates involvement of the nerve to stapedius; accompanying deafness, tinnitus, or vertigo suggests an internal auditory meatus lesion affecting the eighth nerve.

Glossopharyngeal neuralgia resembles trigeminal neuralgia but is much less common; pain is paroxysmal and intense, arises in the tonsillar fossa/throat, may radiate to the ear, and is provoked by swallowing or coughing; rarely it triggers bradycardia/asystole, hypotension, and syncope.

Anatomic clustering of cranial nerves yields recognizable syndromes (Table 452-2): jugular foramen (IX, X, XI), cavernous sinus (III, IV, V1, VI), pontocerebellar angle (V, VI, VII, VIII), and retroparotid space (IX, X, XI, XII plus Horner’s).

Cavernous sinus syndrome is frequently life-threatening: orbital/facial pain, orbital swelling, chemosis, fever, ophthalmoplegia (III, IV, VI), and V1 (±V2) trigeminal involvement—cavernous sinus thrombosis from facial/orbital/sinus infection (including mucormycosis in diabetics) is the most common cause and demands early diagnosis.

Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (idiopathic granulomatous cavernous-sinus/orbital inflammation) causes painful ophthalmoparesis with V1/V2 numbness and shows a dramatic response to glucocorticoids, but its picture can be mimicked by sarcoid, vasculitis, IgG4-related disease, lymphoma, and fungal infection—so confirm before attributing to it.

An eleventh-nerve (spinal accessory) palsy causes little overt neck weakness because other muscles assist head turning; detection relies on palpating absent sternocleidomastoid contraction during head turning and on noting a lower shoulder, scapular winging, and inability to abduct the arm beyond 90 degrees.
harrison.pathophysiology: The cranial nerves are 12 paired nerves with mixed motor, sensory, and autonomic functions linked by their close brainstem relationships; nine connect directly to brainstem nuclei, while CN I and II are effectively brain fiber tracts and CN XI arises largely from upper cervical cord. In trigeminal neuralgia, symptoms arise from ectopic action-potential generation in pain-sensitive afferents of the fifth-nerve root just proximal to its entry at the lateral pons; demyelination of large myelinated (non-nociceptive) fibers renders them hyperexcitable and electrically coupled to adjacent small unmyelinated/poorly myelinated pain fibers, so tactile input can ignite paroxysms of pain. Compression of the root by a blood vessel—most often the superior cerebellar artery (or a tortuous vein)—is implicated in most cases; age-related brain sagging and increased vascular tortuosity may explain its predilection for later life. The trigeminal nerve carries oligodendrocyte-derived (central-type) myelin for up to ~7 mm beyond the brainstem, which may underlie trigeminal neuralgia in MS. In Bell’s palsy there is inflammation of the facial nerve with mononuclear cell infiltration suggesting an infectious/immune mechanism; reactivation of herpes simplex virus type 1 in the geniculate ganglion is thought to cause most cases, with varicella-zoster reactivation implicated in up to one-third (Ramsay Hunt syndrome). The vagus and other lower cranial nerves can be injured along their medullary, meningeal, foraminal, or extracranial courses; the recurrent laryngeal nerve (especially the left) is most often damaged by intrathoracic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Migraine and cluster headache (deep, steady pain rather than superficial stabbing; cluster-tic overlap exists)
Temporal (giant cell) arteritis (superficial facial pain with myalgias/systemic symptoms and elevated ESR/CRP)
Short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache (SUNCT/SUNA) and paroxysmal hemicrania
Dental, jaw, or sinus disease as a source of face pain
Trigeminal neuropathy from tumor (meningioma, schwannoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, metastasis), Sjögren’s/connective-tissue disease, sarcoidosis, leprosy
Supranuclear facial palsy from stroke/structural hemispheric lesion (forehead-sparing, often with limb weakness or aphasia)
Lyme disease facial palsy (unilateral or bilateral) in endemic areas
Guillain-Barré syndrome (often bilateral facial palsy; Fisher variant with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia)
Myasthenia gravis for pure motor cranial weakness without atrophy
Polymyositis/dermatomyositis and myotonic dystrophy mimicking vagal dysphagia/dysphonia
Progressive bulbar palsy (motor neuron disease) for multiple lower cranial motor involvement
infectionMimics: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate herpes zoster) mimicking Bell’s palsy, with auricular/pharyngeal vesicles and often eighth-nerve involvement
Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) causing uni- or bilateral facial palsy
Herpes zoster involving the trigeminal ganglion (acute or postherpetic) or lower cranial nerves
Leprosy involving the facial or trigeminal nerve
Chronic/carcinomatous meningitis, tuberculosis, otitis media/mastoiditis spread to the semilunar ganglion
Diphtheria affecting the pharyngeal branches of the vagus (nasal voice, nasal regurgitation)
Mucormycosis and other invasive fungal infections at the cavernous sinus/orbital apex (especially in diabetics)
nonInfectiousMimics: Sarcoidosis (often bilateral facial palsy; cause of multiple cranial neuropathy)
Tolosa-Hunt syndrome and other idiopathic granulomatous orbital/cavernous inflammation
IgG4-related disease, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and other vasculitides
Lymphoma and metastatic/locally infiltrating tumors (nasopharyngeal carcinoma, neurofibroma, meningioma, chordoma, cholesteatoma)
Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome (recurrent facial palsy, recurrent facial/labial edema, fissured tongue)
Diabetes mellitus, amyloidosis, and connective-tissue/collagen-vascular disease (e.g., Sjögren’s, SLE, scleroderma, MCTD)
Skull-base and posterior-fossa structural lesions (acoustic neuroma, platybasia, basilar invagination, Paget’s disease, Chiari malformation)
Temporal bone fracture or blunt head injury
Iatrogenic/traumatic injury (neck surgery, jugular vein cannulation, carotid endarterectomy/dissection, post-intubation Tapia syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: ESR and/or CRP when temporal arteritis is suspected as a cause of facial pain or in atypical facial palsy
Neuroimaging (MRI/MR angiography) to exclude secondary causes of trigeminal neuralgia and to map the relationship of the fifth-nerve root to adjacent vessels for surgical planning

MRI of the facial nerve, which in idiopathic Bell’s palsy often shows smooth linear enhancement and swelling of the geniculate ganglion and facial nerve (genu, tympanic, mastoid segments); similar enhancement can occur in Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, and perineural malignant spread
Electromyography for prognosis in Bell’s palsy (denervation evident after 10 days indicates axonal degeneration and a longer, possibly incomplete recovery)
In atypical/uncertain facial palsy: testing for diabetes mellitus, Lyme serology, HIV serology, ACE level with chest imaging for sarcoidosis, and lumbar puncture if Guillain-Barré is suspected
Lumbar puncture/CSF examination (mild CSF lymphocytosis may occur in Bell’s palsy; useful for meningeal/inflammatory causes)
Laryngoscopy and chest/mediastinal imaging for vocal cord palsy to evaluate intrathoracic causes of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury
Biopsy when granulomatous/infiltrative cavernous sinus or orbital apex disease (e.g., Tolosa-Hunt mimics, IgG4-related disease) is suspected
redFlags: Objective trigeminal sensory loss, jaw weakness, or jaw deviation accompanying facial pain (suggests structural trigeminal neuropathy rather than classic neuralgia)
Bilateral trigeminal neuralgia or onset in a young adult (consider multiple sclerosis)
Isolated numbness over the chin (mental neuropathy), which can be the sole manifestation of systemic malignancy
Forehead-sparing facial weakness with limb weakness or aphasia (central/supranuclear lesion such as stroke)
Facial palsy with vesicles in the ear canal/palate, severe pain, or eighth-nerve signs (Ramsay Hunt syndrome)
Slowly progressive or insidious facial weakness (suggests tumor invading the temporal bone rather than Bell’s palsy)
Orbital/facial pain with orbital swelling, chemosis, fever, and ophthalmoplegia (cavernous sinus thrombosis—life-threatening)
Glossopharyngeal neuralgia with bradycardia, asystole, hypotension, or syncope
Successive involvement of multiple cranial nerves, especially with bone erosion or foraminal enlargement (infiltrating tumor, granulomatous or neoplastic meningitis)
Corneal anesthesia (loss of V1 corneal sensation) increasing risk of ulceration (neurokeratitis)
harrison.prognosis: Trigeminal neuralgia characteristically remits spontaneously after bouts lasting weeks to months, and remissions can be long-lasting, though the disorder ultimately recurs in most patients. In Bell’s palsy, about 80% of patients recover within a few weeks to months; incomplete paralysis during the first week is the most favorable prognostic sign, whereas EMG evidence of denervation after 10 days predicts axonal degeneration with delayed (typically ~3 months) and possibly incomplete recovery, and recurrences occur in roughly 7% of cases. Idiopathic trigeminal neuropathy usually recovers gradually. Most patients with isolated spinal accessory neuropathy recover. Post-intubation Tapia syndrome (vagal plus hypoglossal palsy) usually resolves within a few months.
pitfalls: Diagnosing classic trigeminal neuralgia despite objective trigeminal sensory loss—such findings indicate trigeminal neuropathy from a structural/secondary cause (aneurysm, neurofibroma, acoustic schwannoma, meningioma).
Overlooking multiple sclerosis as the cause of trigeminal neuralgia in a young adult or when symptoms are bilateral.
Mistaking a central (supranuclear) forehead-sparing facial weakness for peripheral Bell’s palsy and missing a stroke or hemispheric lesion.
Failing to examine the eighth and other cranial nerves in a patient with facial palsy—the eighth nerve runs close to the facial nerve at the pontomedullary junction and in the temporal bone.
Attributing an insidious, progressive facial weakness to Bell’s palsy when it actually reflects a temporal bone or pontine tumor.
Missing Ramsay Hunt syndrome by not inspecting the external auditory canal and palate for zoster vesicles.
Misdiagnosing vagal/laryngeal or pharyngeal muscle disease (polymyositis, dermatomyositis, myotonic dystrophy) as a primary vagus nerve lesion in dysphagia/dysphonia.
Searching intracranially for an isolated vocal cord palsy when intrathoracic disease (aortic aneurysm, enlarged left atrium, mediastinal/bronchial tumor) is the far more common cause.
Delaying recognition and treatment of cavernous sinus thrombosis, an early-diagnosis emergency.
harrison.severityClassification: No formal grading scale is presented in this chapter. In Bell’s palsy, clinical severity is gauged by completeness of paralysis, with incomplete paralysis in the first week being the most favorable prognostic indicator and electromyographic denervation after 10 days indicating axonal degeneration and a worse, more prolonged recovery. The diagnosis of Bell’s palsy is supported clinically by a typical presentation, absence of other risk factors/symptoms, no zoster lesions in the ear canal, and a normal neurologic examination apart from the facial nerve.
